title: Alternating quotients of knot groups
W: The trefoil's group maps onto every alternating group A_n with n>=9, because modulo its centre it is the modular group. Show that every nontrivial knot group maps onto A_n for all large n, or at least for infinitely many n, and bound the last exception in terms of the knot.
M: Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial knot and $G_K=\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$. (a) Prove that $G_K$ surjects onto $A_n$ for all $n\ge N(K)$, and bound $N(K)$ in terms of the crossing number. (b) Weaker: prove that $G_K$ surjects onto $A_n$ for infinitely many $n$, or even for one $n\ge5$. Data (exhaustive search over pairs of conjugate even permutations, meridians $x,y$ with $wx=yw$): for the trefoil ($w=xy$) a surjection exists exactly for $n=5$ and $n\ge9$, since every surjection kills the centre and factors through $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)\cong C_2*C_3$, and Miller proved $(2,3)$-generation of $A_n$ for $n\ne3,6,7,8$. For the figure-eight knot ($w=x^{-1}yxy^{-1}$) a surjection exists for $n=6,9,10$ and not for $n=5,7,8$. Is $N(4_1)=9$, i.e. does $G_{4_1}$ surject onto $A_n$ for every $n\ge9$?
why: Dunfield and Thurston asked whether every finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold group has an alternating quotient; whether this holds for infinitely many or all large n is also open, and Fuchsian groups are known to have all large alternating quotients (Everitt, Liebeck-Shalev). Knot complements are the most concrete test case: their groups are normally generated by a meridian and are strongly constrained, and an answer would clarify what finite quotients knot groups have, which matters for profinite rigidity.
issues: Special case of open questions: Dunfield-Thurston Question 7.6 (existence of an A_n quotient for hyperbolic 3-manifolds), and Button (arXiv 1010.2726) notes it is unknown whether such manifolds have A_n quotients for infinitely many or all but finitely many n. So it is not fully novel, but the knot-group formulation with an effective N(K) does not appear in what I found. Verified by computer: the trefoil gives n=5 yes, n=6,7 no; the figure-eight gives n=5,7,8 no and n=6,9 yes. Checked the trefoil argument (the centre (xy)^3 must map trivially). Torus knots follow from Everitt's theorem on free products of cyclic groups. Added the weaker form (b), since even it appears open for hyperbolic knots.

title: Finding Huang's vertex
W: Huang's theorem says that any set of more than half the corners of the n-cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours in the set. When the set is listed by a small circuit, how hard is it to find such a corner, or a flaw in the listing? The problem is easily shown to be at least as hard as the pigeonhole class PPP. Is it in PPP, so that it is PPP-complete, or does Huang's linear-algebra proof make it harder?
M: $\mathrm{HUANG}$: given a Boolean circuit $f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^n$, with inputs read as elements of $[2^{n-1}+1]$ and inputs beyond $2^{n-1}+1$ ignored, output either $i\ne j$ with $f(i)=f(j)$, or $i,j_1,\dots,j_m$ with $m=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil$ such that $f(j_1),\dots,f(j_m)$ are distinct and each is at Hamming distance $1$ from $f(i)$. By Huang's theorem this problem is total. It is PPP-hard: embed a PIGEON instance so that every image has even weight, which forces every solution to be a collision. Is $\mathrm{HUANG}\in\mathrm{PPP}$? If not, which standard TFNP class (for example one defined by a linear-algebra principle) contains it, and is it complete for that class?
why: Huang's proof of the sensitivity conjecture is purely spectral, and no combinatorial proof is known. Placing the associated search problem in PPP would amount to a pigeonhole-style, efficiently checkable version of the argument. Showing it lies outside PPP in the black-box model would separate the theorem from counting principles. It is a natural test case for the recent programme of classifying TFNP problems that come from extremal combinatorics (Ramsey, iterated pigeonhole, linear-algebra classes).
issues: My attack: HUANG is PPP-hard. Pad a PIGEON instance with 2^m pigeons and 2^m-1 holes to 2^{n-1}+1 pigeons and 2^{n-1} holes (n-1=m+1, dummy pigeons mapped injectively to dummy holes), and send the holes to even-weight strings. The image then has no cube edges, so every solution is a collision. So 'Is HUANG in FP?' is answered (no, unless PPP is in FP). The question is really about membership in PPP, and I rewrote M around that. Containment in PPA or PLS would put PPP inside those classes, which is unlikely. I found no paper on the TFNP complexity of Huang's theorem. Laplante–Naserasr–Sunny–Wang (2026) give a linear-dependence proof, which may suggest a linear-algebra class.

title: Forced blow-up up to the Lions threshold
W: With an ordinary Laplacian, a smooth compactly supported push can make a fluid at rest blow up in finite time (OpenAI, 2026). With dissipation (-Δ)^α for α ≥ 5/4, Lions proved that solutions stay smooth. Does forced blow-up from rest still happen for every α strictly between 1 and 5/4?
M:
For $\alpha\in(1,5/4)$ consider $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u+
abla p=-(-\Delta)^{\alpha}u+f$, $
abla\cdot u=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$, $u(\cdot,0)=0$. Decide whether for every such $\alpha$ there is $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3	imes(0,\infty);\mathbb R^3)$ for which the smooth solution breaks down in finite time, i.e. $\limsup_{t\uparrow T}\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}=\infty$ for some $T<\infty$.
why: Lions' threshold $\alpha=5/4$ is exactly where energy-level dissipation becomes critical, so it is the natural candidate for the sharp boundary between regularity and singularity. The 2026 construction of forced blow-up at $\alpha=1$ makes the forced form of this question meaningful. Pushing it to every $\alpha<5/4$ would show that the energy-critical exponent is the true dividing line, at least when forcing is allowed.
issues: As written the range '$\alpha<5/4$' included $\alpha=1$, which is a form of Clay's forced statement and was claimed in 2026 by OpenAI. That paper proves smooth, compactly supported, time-dependent force, zero data, all $\nu>0$, not yet refereed. Cao–Chi–Nie use it as a black box. I restricted to $\alpha\in(1,5/4)$ and changed 'construct' to 'decide'. Hypodissipative forced blow-up is known for $\alpha<\alpha_0\approx0.093$ with a rougher force (arXiv:2407.06776). None of the sources treat $\alpha>1$ or mention Lions' threshold. Breakdown is defined via $L^\infty$.

title: Is the Mandelbrot set decidable at Gaussian rationals?
W: Is there an algorithm that takes a complex number with rational real and imaginary parts and decides whether it lies in the Mandelbrot set? Escaping points can be confirmed, and so can points that have an attracting or neutral cycle of some period, since for each period that is an exact algebraic check. The trouble is points on the boundary where every cycle repels. No such Gaussian rational is known, but none has been ruled out.
M: Let $M=\{c\in\mathbb C:(f_c^{n}(0))_{n\ge0}\text{ bounded}\}$, $f_c(z)=z^2+c$. Prove or disprove that $M\cap\mathbb Q(i)$ is a decidable subset of $\mathbb Q(i)$ (with the standard encoding of Gaussian rationals). Since $\mathbb Q(i)\setminus M$ is recursively enumerable, and for each $n$ the existence of an $n$-cycle of $f_c$ with multiplier of modulus $\le1$ is decidable for algebraic $c$ (Tarski), a positive answer would follow from: (*) every $c\in M\cap\mathbb Q(i)$ has a non-repelling cycle. Prove or disprove (*). (Example: $c=\mu/2-\mu^2/4=(37+16i)/100$ with $\mu=(3+4i)/5$ has a fixed point of multiplier $\mu$, not a root of unity, so $c\in\partial M$. Centres and Misiurewicz parameters are algebraic integers, so the only ones in $\mathbb Q(i)$ lie in $\mathbb Z[i]$.)
why: M is not decidable in the Blum–Shub–Smale model, and its computability as a set (Hertling) is tied to the density-of-hyperbolicity conjecture. Restricting to exact rational inputs gives the most concrete version of 'can a computer decide the Mandelbrot set?', and leads to an arithmetic-dynamics question: can a non-escaping Gaussian rational have only repelling cycles (be non-hyperbolic, e.g. infinitely renormalizable or Collet–Eckmann-like)?
issues: Not novel: Potgieter, 'Hypercomputing the Mandelbrot set?' (arXiv cs/0604003, Sect. 2.3 'A rational refuge?') asks exactly whether M ∩ Q^2 is decidable, leaves it open and guesses no. Found no later resolution. Added the reduction to (*) (escape semi-decidable; non-repelling cycle of given period decidable for algebraic c), which shows the real difficulty. Verified the example computation. Real rationals are trivial (M ∩ R = [-2, 1/4]), so only non-real Gaussian rationals matter. The multiplier (3+4i)/5 = e^{2πiθ} has θ Diophantine by Baker's theorem, so that example is a Siegel parameter.
